title: Hing-Tempered Dal Tadka
description: Creamy yellow lentils finished with a sizzling asafoetida and cumin tempering.
intro: The dish that convinces people no-allium cooking loses nothing. All the savory depth here comes from asafoetida bloomed in hot ghee — it turns nutty and garlicky the moment it hits the fat.
swapNote: Asafoetida (hing) does the work garlic normally would; ginger and tomato supply the sweetness you'd get from onion.
steps: Simmer the dal with water and turmeric until completely soft and breaking down, about 20 minutes (or 3 whistles in a pressure cooker). Whisk until creamy and keep warm.
Heat the ghee in a small pan over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 15 seconds.
Add the asafoetida — it will foam and smell savory almost immediately. Follow with ginger and green chili and cook 30 seconds.
Add the tomato, chili powder, and a pinch of salt. Cook until the tomato collapses into a thick paste, 4–5 minutes.
Pour the tempering into the dal, add salt to taste, and simmer together 5 minutes so the flavors marry.
Finish with fresh coriander and serve with rice or roti.
tips: Add the asafoetida off-heat for a second if your pan runs hot — it turns bitter if it scorches.
A squeeze of lemon at the table lifts the whole bowl.

title: Jain Vegetable Kofta Curry
description: Bottle gourd dumplings simmered in a silky tomato-cashew gravy.
intro: A celebration dish built entirely without onion, garlic, or root vegetables — proof that Jain cooking can be as rich as any restaurant curry.
swapNote: Soaked cashews give the body onion paste usually provides; ginger and garam masala carry the aroma.

ingredients.name: bottle gourd (lauki), grated and squeezed dry

steps: Mix the squeezed bottle gourd with chickpea flour, garam masala, and salt. It should just hold together — add a spoonful more flour if wet.
Roll into walnut-sized balls and shallow-fry over medium heat until golden all over. Drain on paper and set aside.
Blend the soaked cashews with a splash of water into a completely smooth cream.
Heat ghee in a wide pan, add asafoetida and ginger, and cook 30 seconds. Add the tomato puree, coriander, and turmeric.
Cook the puree down until it darkens and the ghee separates at the edges, 10–12 minutes — this step is what builds depth.
Stir in the cashew cream and 1 cup water, simmer 5 minutes, then swirl in the cream and salt.
Add the koftas just before serving so they stay tender, not soggy.
tips: Squeeze the gourd hard — wet batter means koftas that fall apart in the oil.
Drop the koftas in at the table if you're making the gravy ahead.

title: No-Onion Paneer Butter Masala
description: The restaurant classic rebuilt on tomato, cashew, and butter — no allium at all.
intro: Most butter masala leans on onion paste for sweetness. This version gets there with slow-cooked tomato, soaked cashews, and a pinch of sugar, which is how many temple kitchens have always made it.
swapNote: Long-cooked tomato plus cashew replaces the onion base entirely; asafoetida stands in for garlic.
steps: Simmer the tomatoes and cashews with 1/2 cup water until the tomatoes are completely soft, about 15 minutes. Cool slightly and blend into a silky puree, then strain for a truly smooth gravy.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a heavy pan. Add asafoetida and ginger and cook 30 seconds without browning.
Pour in the tomato-cashew puree — stand back, it spits. Add chili powder, sugar, and salt.
Simmer uncovered 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until the gravy thickens and turns a deeper red.
Stir in garam masala, crushed kasuri methi, cream, and the remaining butter.
Fold in the paneer and warm through for 3 minutes — don't boil it or the paneer toughens.
tips: Soak the paneer in hot salted water for 10 minutes first; it stays soft in the gravy.
Straining the puree is the difference between homestyle and restaurant texture.

title: Sattvic Palak Paneer
description: Bright green spinach gravy with soft paneer, kept vivid by a quick blanch.
intro: The secret to green — not khaki — palak paneer is blanching the spinach for exactly two minutes and shocking it in ice water before blending.
swapNote: Ginger and green chili carry the heat that garlic usually would; hing adds the savory bottom note.
steps: Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 2 minutes, then plunge into ice water. Drain well.
Blend the spinach with the green chilies into a coarse puree — leave a little texture.
Heat ghee, crackle the cumin seeds, then add asafoetida and ginger. Cook 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and cook until soft and jammy, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the spinach puree, salt, and a splash of water. Simmer just 5 minutes — longer dulls the color.
Add garam masala, cream, and the paneer. Warm through and serve immediately.
tips: Never cover the pan after the spinach goes in; trapped steam turns it olive-drab.
Pan-sear the paneer cubes first if you like a firmer bite.

title: No-Onion Chana Masala
description: Tangy chickpea curry built on tomato, amchur, and toasted whole spices.
intro: Chana masala is one of the easiest curries to make allium-free because its signature flavor was never onion — it's the sour-smoky combination of amchur, anardana, and toasted cumin.
swapNote: Dried mango powder and pomegranate seed do the heavy lifting; no onion base needed at all.

ingredients.name: Fresh coriander and lemon, to finish

steps: Heat the oil and crackle the cumin seeds, then add asafoetida and half the ginger.
Add the tomato puree, ground coriander, chili powder, and salt. Cook down hard, 12–15 minutes, until the oil separates.
Add the chickpeas and 1 cup water. Simmer 15 minutes so they absorb the masala.
Mash a few chickpeas against the side of the pan to thicken the gravy naturally.
Stir in amchur and chana masala, cook 2 more minutes.
Top with the remaining raw ginger, fresh coriander, and a hard squeeze of lemon.
tips: A black tea bag dropped in while the chickpeas simmer gives the classic dark color.
This tastes better on day two — make it ahead.

title: No-Onion Rajma (Kidney Bean Curry)
description: Slow-simmered kidney beans in a thick, warming tomato-ginger gravy.
intro: The creaminess in good rajma comes from beans breaking down, not from onion. Cook them long enough and the gravy thickens itself.
swapNote: Mashed beans supply the body; hing and ginger supply the savory aroma.
steps: Pressure-cook the soaked beans with salt and water until completely tender — they should squash easily between your fingers.
Heat the oil, crackle the cumin, add asafoetida and ginger.
Add the tomato puree with coriander, turmeric, and chili powder. Cook until thick and glossy, about 15 minutes.
Add the beans along with their cooking liquid. Simmer uncovered 20 minutes.
Mash about a quarter of the beans against the pan to thicken the gravy.
Finish with garam masala and rest 10 minutes off heat before serving over rice.
tips: Undercooked kidney beans are both unpleasant and unsafe — cook them fully soft.
The gravy should coat a spoon; if it's thin, simmer longer uncovered.

title: No-Onion Sambar
description: Tamarind-soured lentil stew loaded with vegetables and curry leaves.
intro: Traditional temple sambar has never used onion. The sourness of tamarind and the aroma of a curry-leaf tempering are the whole point.
swapNote: Tamarind and sambar powder define the flavor; a curry-leaf and mustard tempering replaces any aromatics.
steps: Cook the dal with turmeric until completely soft, then whisk smooth.
Separately simmer the vegetables with tamarind paste, sambar powder, salt, and 2 cups water until just tender.
Combine the vegetables with the dal and simmer 10 minutes so it thickens slightly.
For the tempering, heat oil until shimmering. Add mustard seeds and wait for them to pop.
Add dried chilies, curry leaves, and asafoetida — it will crackle violently for a few seconds.
Pour the tempering over the sambar, cover for 2 minutes to trap the aroma, then stir and garnish with coriander.
tips: Add okra separately at the end so it doesn't turn slimy.
The tempering is not optional — it's where 80% of the flavor lives.

title: Cumin & Curry Leaf Poha
description: Flattened rice tossed with mustard seeds, peanuts, peas, and lemon.
intro: A fifteen-minute breakfast that's naturally allium-free in its simplest form. The trick is rinsing the poha briefly — soak it and you get porridge.
swapNote: Mustard seeds, curry leaves, and peanuts build all the savoriness; lemon does the brightening onion might.
steps: Rinse the poha in a colander under running water for 20 seconds, then let it drain and fluff. It should be damp, never soggy.
Heat the oil, toast the peanuts until golden, and set them aside.
In the same oil, pop the mustard seeds, add cumin, curry leaves, and green chili.
Add the peas and turmeric with a splash of water; cook 3 minutes until tender.
Fold in the poha gently with salt and sugar. Warm through 2 minutes, covered.
Off heat, add lemon juice, the peanuts, and plenty of coriander.
tips: Turmeric goes into the oil, not onto the poha — it coats more evenly.
Sugar isn't optional; it balances the lemon.

title: Vegetable Rava Upma
description: Fluffy semolina with carrots, peas, ginger, and a mustard-seed tempering.
intro: Upma gets a bad reputation only because it's usually made badly. Toast the semolina properly and use exactly 1:2.5 semolina to water and it comes out light every time.
swapNote: Ginger, green chili, and curry leaves provide the aromatics — no onion needed for a savory base.
steps: Dry-toast the semolina in a pan over medium heat until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker, 5 minutes. Tip it out.
Heat ghee, pop the mustard seeds, add urad dal and fry until golden.
Add curry leaves, ginger, and chili, then the vegetables. Cook 4 minutes.
Pour in the water with salt and bring to a rolling boil.
Lower the heat and rain in the semolina with one hand while stirring constantly with the other — this prevents lumps.
Cover and steam 3 minutes, then fluff with a fork and finish with lemon and coriander.
tips: Toasting is the whole game. Untoasted semolina makes a gluey upma.
Add a spoon of ghee at the end for the glossy restaurant finish.

title: Besan Chilla (Chickpea Pancakes)
description: Savory chickpea-flour pancakes studded with grated vegetables.
intro: High-protein, naturally gluten-free, and ready in twenty minutes. Chilla is the no-allium cook's answer to an omelette.
swapNote: Ajwain (carom seed) and ginger give the batter its savory bite where onion is usually grated in.
steps: Whisk the chickpea flour with water into a smooth batter the thickness of heavy cream. Let it rest 10 minutes.
Stir in the vegetables, ginger, chili, ajwain, asafoetida, turmeric, and salt.
Heat a griddle over medium and brush with oil. Pour a ladle of batter and spread into a round.
Drizzle oil around the edges and cook until the underside is golden and lacy, 3 minutes.
Flip and cook 2 minutes more until cooked through.
Serve hot with coconut chutney or plain yogurt.
tips: Rest the batter — it hydrates the flour and stops a raw, chalky taste.
Medium heat only; high heat browns the outside before the inside sets.

title: Crispy Rava Dosa
description: Lacy, shatteringly crisp semolina crepes — no fermentation needed.
intro: The fastest dosa there is: no grinding, no overnight ferment. The batter must be shockingly thin, which is what creates the lace.
swapNote: Cumin, pepper, and curry leaves season the batter in place of the usual chopped onion.
steps: Whisk all three flours with the water — the batter should be as thin as milk. Rest 20 minutes.
Stir in cumin, pepper, curry leaves, ginger, and salt. Whisk again; the flours settle constantly.
Heat a pan until quite hot. Pour the batter from a height in a circular motion — do not spread it with the ladle.
The batter will spread itself into a lacy net with holes. Drizzle oil around the edges.
Cook undisturbed until the edges lift and the dosa is deep golden and crisp, 3–4 minutes.
Fold and serve immediately with coconut chutney.
tips: Whisk before every single dosa — the batter separates in under a minute.
If your dosa comes out solid instead of lacy, the batter is too thick. Add water.

title: Jeera Vegetable Pulao
description: Fragrant basmati simmered with whole spices, cumin, and garden vegetables.
intro: Whole spices bloomed in ghee perfume the entire pot. This is the dish that proves aromatics don't have to mean alliums.
swapNote: Whole garam spices — bay, clove, cinnamon, cumin — carry the aroma from start to finish.

ingredients.name: basmati rice, rinsed and soaked 20 minutes

steps: Heat the ghee and add all the whole spices. Wait until the cumin sizzles and the cinnamon unfurls its scent, about 45 seconds.
Add the ginger and the vegetables; sauté 3 minutes.
Drain the rice and add it, stirring gently for 2 minutes to coat every grain in ghee.
Add the water and salt, bring to a hard boil, then cover and reduce to the lowest heat.
Cook undisturbed 12 minutes. Do not lift the lid.
Rest off heat 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork from the edges inward.
tips: Soaking the rice is what gives you long, separate grains.
Stirring cooked rice breaks it — always fluff with a fork, never a spoon.

title: Lemon Rice (Chitranna)
description: Leftover rice transformed with turmeric, peanuts, curry leaves, and lemon.
intro: The great South Indian lunchbox dish, and the best possible use for yesterday's rice. Naturally free of onion and garlic in every traditional version.
swapNote: Toasted dals and peanuts add crunch and savor; lemon supplies all the brightness.
steps: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds.
Add both dals and the peanuts; fry patiently until everything is golden — this crunch is the dish's signature.
Add curry leaves, dried chilies, turmeric, and asafoetida. Stand back; it spits.
Turn off the heat completely, then add the lemon juice and salt to the tempering.
Fold in the cooled rice gently until every grain is yellow.
Taste and adjust lemon — it should be assertively tangy.
tips: Cold, day-old rice works far better than fresh, which turns to mush.
Adding lemon off the heat keeps it bright instead of bitter.

title: Curd Rice (Thayir Sadam)
description: Cooling yogurt rice with a mustard tempering, ginger, and pomegranate.
intro: The most soothing thing in the South Indian repertoire, and the classic ending to a meal. Cooling by design — exactly the kind of food sattvic eating favors.
swapNote: Ginger and green chili in the tempering are the only aromatics this dish has ever needed.

ingredients.name: cooked rice, slightly overcooked and mashed

steps: Mash the warm rice lightly with the back of a spoon until it's soft and slightly broken down.
Let it cool to room temperature — hot rice will split the yogurt.
Fold in the yogurt, milk, and salt. It should be loose; it thickens as it sits.
Heat oil, pop the mustard seeds, fry the urad dal golden, then add curry leaves, ginger, chili, and asafoetida.
Pour the tempering over the rice and fold it through.
Top with pomegranate seeds and coriander. Serve cool or at room temperature.
tips: Make it looser than you think — it firms up considerably in the fridge.
Pomegranate isn't traditional everywhere, but the pops of sweetness are wonderful.

title: Baked Vegetable Samosas
description: Crisp baked pastry filled with spiced peas, carrot, and potato.
intro: Classic samosa filling was never about onion — it's the amchur and roasted cumin that make it taste like a samosa.
swapNote: Amchur, roasted cumin, and ginger define the filling; no onion required.
steps: Heat the oil, crackle the cumin and crushed coriander seeds, then add ginger and chili.
Add the peas with a splash of water and cook until tender, 5 minutes.
Fold in the crushed potato, amchur, garam masala, and salt. Cook 3 minutes, then cool completely.
Fill each pastry sheet, fold into a cone, and seal the edge with a flour-water paste.
Brush generously with oil and bake at 200°C (400°F) for 22–25 minutes, turning once, until deep golden.
Serve with tamarind or coriander chutney.
tips: Cool the filling fully or the pastry goes soggy and tears.
For a Jain version, swap the potato for crumbled paneer or green banana.

title: Crunchy Masala Peanuts
description: Chickpea-flour-coated peanuts baked until shatteringly crisp.
intro: The teatime snack that disappears fastest. Baking instead of deep-frying makes them keep for a week without going soft.
swapNote: Chaat masala and amchur bring the tang; no onion or garlic powder anywhere.
steps: Sprinkle the peanuts with just enough water to dampen them — about 2 tablespoons.
Add both flours, all the spices, and salt. Toss until every peanut wears a thin, even coat.
Drizzle over the oil and toss again. The mix should be crumbly, not pasty.
Spread in a single layer on a lined tray.
Bake at 180°C (350°F) for 20 minutes, shaking the tray every 5 minutes so they brown evenly.
Cool completely before eating — they crisp up as they cool.
tips: They will seem slightly soft straight from the oven. Trust the cooling.
Store airtight; they stay crisp about a week.

title: Sabudana Khichdi
description: Pearly tapioca tossed with crushed peanuts, potato, and green chili.
intro: A fasting-day staple, which is precisely why it contains no onion or garlic — fasting foods in Indian tradition exclude both by definition.
swapNote: Roasted peanut powder gives richness and body; cumin and chili do the seasoning.

ingredients.name: sago pearls (sabudana), soaked 4 hours and drained

steps: Soak the sago until each pearl squashes easily between your fingers, then drain thoroughly and rest uncovered 30 minutes.
Toss the drained sago with the ground peanuts, sugar, and salt so the pearls are coated and separate.
Heat the ghee, crackle the cumin, add the green chilies and potato.
Cover and cook the potato until tender and lightly golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the sago mixture and toss gently over medium heat until the pearls turn translucent, 4–5 minutes.
Finish with lemon and coriander; serve immediately while it's springy.
tips: Overcooking turns sago into glue — stop as soon as the pearls go clear.
The peanut coating is what keeps them from clumping. Don't skip it.

title: Methi Thepla
description: Soft fenugreek flatbreads that keep for days — the classic travel food.
intro: Gujarati thepla is the great travelling bread: it stays soft for two days unrefrigerated, and the traditional recipe has never included onion or garlic.
swapNote: Fresh fenugreek leaves and ajwain provide a savory-bitter depth no allium could match.
steps: Combine everything except the cooking oil and knead into a soft dough, adding water a spoonful at a time. The methi releases moisture, so go slowly.
Rest the dough 20 minutes under a damp cloth.
Divide into 12 balls and roll each as thin as you can manage, dusting with flour.
Cook on a hot griddle until bubbles appear, about 45 seconds.
Flip, brush with oil, and press the edges down with a spatula until brown spots form on both sides.
Stack in a cloth-lined container — the trapped steam keeps them soft.
tips: Thinner rolling gives softer thepla. Thick ones go leathery when cool.
Squeeze bitter methi with a little salt for 10 minutes first if you prefer it mild.

title: Ginger & Green Chili Paratha
description: Flaky layered flatbread with a bright ginger-chili filling.
intro: A stuffed paratha that gets its punch from fresh ginger and chili rather than the onion most street versions use.
swapNote: Raw ginger and green chili give heat and aroma; asafoetida rounds it out.

ingredients.name: Ghee or oil, for layering and cooking

steps: Knead the flour, water, and a pinch of salt into a soft, pliable dough. Rest 20 minutes.
Mix the ginger, chili, asafoetida, ajwain, and salt with 1 tbsp ghee into a coarse paste.
Roll a dough ball into a small round, spread a thin layer of the paste, and fold into a triangle or roll into a spiral.
Roll out again gently to about 6 inches — don't press so hard the filling bursts.
Cook on a hot griddle, brushing both sides with ghee, until puffed and spotted brown.
Serve hot with yogurt and pickle.
tips: The spiral fold gives the most layers — roll it like a cinnamon bun, then flatten.
Rest the dough properly; unrested dough springs back and tears.

title: Fresh Coconut Chutney
description: The essential dosa companion — coconut, roasted gram, ginger, and curry leaves.
intro: Every South Indian breakfast needs this. The classic recipe contains no allium whatsoever, just coconut, chili, and a hot tempering poured over the top.
swapNote: Roasted gram dal thickens and adds nuttiness; ginger provides the bite.
steps: Blend the coconut, roasted gram, ginger, green chilies, salt, and water into a thick, slightly coarse paste.
Scrape into a serving bowl and adjust the consistency with a little more water.
Heat the coconut oil until shimmering.
Pop the mustard seeds, then add urad dal and fry until golden.
Add the dried chili and curry leaves; they'll crackle for a few seconds.
Pour the hot tempering directly over the chutney and serve without stirring it in.
tips: Roasted gram dal is what keeps the chutney from separating. Cashews work in a pinch.
Make it the same day — fresh coconut sours quickly.

title: Tomato & Ginger Chutney
description: Sweet-sour cooked tomato chutney with a deep ginger backbone.
intro: Cook tomatoes long enough and they develop the same savory depth people chase with onion. This keeps a week in the fridge.
swapNote: Slow-cooked tomato plus a heavy hand with ginger replaces the usual onion-garlic base completely.
steps: Heat the oil and pop the mustard seeds, then add cumin and fenugreek. Fenugreek burns fast — keep it moving.
Add curry leaves, asafoetida, and the ginger; fry 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes, chili powder, and salt.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, for 20 minutes until the tomatoes collapse and the oil pools at the edges.
Stir in the jaggery and cook 2 minutes more.
Cool and store in a jar; it thickens further as it sits.
tips: Don't rush the reduction — this is where the savory depth comes from.
Excellent with dosa, thepla, or simply on toast.

title: Cabbage Thoran
description: Keralan stir-fried cabbage with coconut, curry leaves, and mustard seeds.
intro: A dry, fresh-tasting vegetable side that takes fifteen minutes. The coconut isn't a garnish — it's crushed in with green chili and cumin, and it makes the dish.
swapNote: Crushed coconut with cumin and green chili is the flavor base — the traditional Kerala approach needs no allium.
steps: Crush the coconut, green chilies, cumin seeds, and turmeric together coarsely — a mortar or a few pulses in a processor.
Heat the coconut oil, pop the mustard seeds, and add the curry leaves.
Add the cabbage and salt, and toss over high heat for 2 minutes.
Lower the heat, cover, and steam 5 minutes in the cabbage's own moisture.
Uncover, add the coconut mixture, and toss over medium heat for 3 minutes.
Serve while the cabbage still has a little bite.
tips: Never add water — the cabbage provides plenty and you want a dry finish.
Coconut oil genuinely matters here; other oils taste flat.

title: Cardamom Rice Kheer
description: Slow-simmered milk pudding scented with cardamom, saffron, and pistachio.
intro: There is no shortcut. Kheer is milk, rice, and patience — forty minutes of gentle stirring turns three ingredients into something remarkable.
swapNote: A naturally allium-free dish, as all Indian sweets are.
steps: Warm the saffron in 2 tbsp of the milk and set aside to bloom.
Sauté the drained rice in ghee for 2 minutes — this keeps the grains distinct.
Add the milk and bring to a bare simmer. Cook uncovered on low, stirring every few minutes and scraping the sides, for 35–40 minutes.
The kheer is ready when it coats a spoon and has reduced by about a third.
Add the sugar, cardamom, and saffron milk. Cook 5 minutes more — sugar added earlier prevents the rice from softening.
Stir in most of the nuts, then chill or serve warm, topped with the rest.
tips: Use a heavy-bottomed pan and stir the bottom often, or it will catch and taste scorched.
It thickens a lot as it cools — pull it off looser than you want it.

title: Gajar Halwa (Carrot Pudding)
description: Grated carrots slow-cooked in milk and ghee until jammy and rich.
intro: Winter's great dessert. The transformation from raw grated carrot to deep orange halwa takes about an hour of reduction, and there's no substituting for it.
swapNote: Naturally allium-free — as all traditional Indian sweets are.
steps: Fry the nuts and raisins in 1 tbsp ghee until golden; set aside.
Cook the grated carrots in the milk over medium heat, stirring regularly, until the milk has almost entirely evaporated — 30–35 minutes.
Add the remaining ghee and fry the carrots for 8–10 minutes; they'll darken and start to glisten.
Add the sugar. The mixture will loosen as the sugar melts — keep cooking until it thickens again.
Stir in the cardamom and milk powder if using, and cook 5 minutes more.
Fold in the fried nuts and raisins. Serve warm.
tips: Grate the carrots coarsely; fine grating turns to mush.
The moment the ghee starts separating at the edges, it's done.

title: Besan Ladoo
description: Roasted chickpea flour balls — four ingredients, endless patience.
intro: The entire recipe is besan, ghee, sugar, and cardamom. All the flavor comes from roasting the flour slowly until it turns the color of wet sand and smells nutty.
swapNote: Naturally allium-free; a temple-prasad classic.
steps: Melt the ghee in a heavy pan over low heat and add the chickpea flour.
Roast, stirring almost constantly, for 20–25 minutes. It will go from pale and pasty to loose, sandy, and deeply fragrant.
Do not rush this — under-roasted besan tastes raw and chalky. The color should be golden brown.
Take off the heat and cool until just warm to the touch, about 15 minutes.
Mix in the powdered sugar and cardamom thoroughly. Adding sugar to hot flour makes it melt and go runny.
Roll into walnut-sized balls, press a pistachio on top, and let them firm up for an hour.
tips: If the mix won't hold together, add a spoon of warm melted ghee.
Coarse besan gives the classic grainy texture; fine flour makes them dense.

title: Proper Masala Chai
description: Strong, spiced, milky tea made the way it's actually made at home.
intro: Real chai is boiled, not steeped, and the spices go in whole and crushed fresh. Ginger and cardamom are the non-negotiables.
swapNote: Naturally allium-free.
steps: Bring the water to a boil with the crushed ginger and whole spices. Boil hard for 2 minutes to extract them.
Add the tea leaves and boil 1 minute more — the water should go deep amber.
Add the milk and sugar and bring back to a boil.
When it rises up the pan, pull it off the heat, let it settle, and return it. Do this three times — this is what gives chai its body.
Strain into cups through a fine sieve.
Serve immediately, very hot.
tips: Crush the ginger with the flat of a knife rather than grating; you want its juice, not its fibre.
Boiling three times is genuinely the technique — don't shortcut it.

title: Mango Lassi
description: Thick, cooling yogurt and mango drink with a hint of cardamom.
intro: Cooling, sattvic, and takes ninety seconds. Use Alphonso or Kesar pulp if you can find it — the flavor is entirely different from generic mango.
swapNote: Naturally allium-free.

ingredients.name: Crushed pistachios and saffron, to garnish

steps: Blend the mango, yogurt, milk, sugar, and cardamom until completely smooth.
Taste and adjust — very ripe mangoes may need no sugar at all.
Thin with a splash more milk if you prefer it drinkable rather than spoonable.
Chill for 20 minutes if your ingredients weren't already cold.
Pour into tall glasses and top with pistachios and a few saffron threads.
tips: Never add ice to the blender — it waters down the flavor. Chill the ingredients instead.
A pinch of salt sharpens the mango flavor considerably.

title: Ginger-Cumin Vegetable Stew
description: A gentle one-pot stew leaning on ginger, cumin, and toasted coriander.
intro: The weeknight dish to make when you want something warming and undemanding. Everything goes in one pot and it looks after itself.
swapNote: Toasted whole coriander and a generous amount of ginger build the savory base.
steps: Toast the coriander seeds in a dry pan until fragrant, then crush coarsely.
Heat the oil, crackle the cumin seeds, add asafoetida and ginger.
Add the crushed coriander and turmeric, then the vegetables. Toss to coat.
Pour in the broth, season, and simmer covered until everything is tender, about 20 minutes.
Stir in the coconut milk and warm through without boiling.
Finish with lemon juice and plenty of fresh coriander.
tips: Add quick-cooking vegetables like peas in the last 5 minutes only.
Toasting and crushing the coriander yourself is a noticeable upgrade over pre-ground.
